does: Rolls a ball of atta dough into a thin, even round, a little at a time, turning it often, so that it is the same thickness all over and puffs evenly when it is cooked.
how: Flatten a ball of dough in a dish of dry flour, coating both faces lightly.
Roll from the centre outwards with short, firm strokes. Give the dough a small turn after each stroke, so that it grows into a round.
Use just enough flour to stop it sticking. Shake off the extra, because burnt flour makes a bitter smell on the hot plate.
Stop when the round is thin and even from the middle to the edge, with no thick patches or tears.
Cook it at once. A rolled round that waits dries at the edge and tears when lifted.

cues.text: The round is even in thickness and has a smooth edge with no cracks.
It peels from the board without sticking and does not tear.

mistakes.mistake: Rolling thick in the middle and thin at the edge, so that it cooks unevenly and does not puff.
mistakes.fix: Roll from the centre outwards and turn the dough after every stroke.

mistakes.mistake: Using too much dry flour, which burns on the hot plate.
mistakes.fix: Dust lightly and shake off what is not needed.

mistakes.mistake: Stacking rolled rounds without flour, so that they stick.
mistakes.fix: Cook each one as it is rolled.

comes_after.why: The rounds are rolled from a rested atta dough, so the dough comes first.

variant_of.differs: Each round is rolled alone, from a small ball, and cooked at once. The dough is soft and unrested between rolls. The aim is a thin, even disc that will puff, and not a sheet that holds its shape and is cut.
